lead: Schedulers are judged by measurable performance criteria. The criteria tell us how well the CPU is used, how many jobs finish, and how long users wait. They are needed to compare different scheduling policies and to pick a policy that fits the system’s goals, such as keeping a web server responsive or maximizing batch throughput.

blocks.text: CPU utilization is the percentage of time the processor is busy. It is computed as (busy time ÷ total time) × 100 %.
Throughput is the number of jobs completed per hour. Higher throughput means the system finishes more work in the same period.
Turnaround time for a process = completion time – arrival time. It measures the total time a job spends in the system.
Waiting time = total time a process spends in the ready queue. It is turnaround time minus the CPU burst time.
Response time = time of first CPU allocation – arrival time. It matters for interactive tasks where the user expects a quick reaction.

items: All metrics are expressed in milliseconds (ms) for short jobs or seconds (s) for long jobs.
Metrics can be averaged over many processes to obtain system‑wide values.

blocks.text: In a non‑preemptive policy the CPU runs a process until it either finishes or blocks. The scheduler cannot take the CPU away voluntarily.
In a preemptive policy the scheduler may interrupt a running process, for example when a shorter job arrives (shortest‑remaining‑time) or when a time slice expires (round robin).

items: When a process arrives, place it in the ready queue.
If the scheduler is preemptive, compare the new process with the running one.
If the new process has higher priority (or shorter remaining burst), save the state of the current process and dispatch the new one.
Otherwise let the current process continue until it blocks or finishes.

blocks.text: Non‑preemptive scheduling gives low context‑switch overhead but can cause long waiting for short, interactive jobs. Preemptive scheduling improves responsiveness at the cost of more overhead.
Avg. waiting time = Σ waiting_i ÷ n
blocks.where: waiting_i is the waiting time of process i; n is the number of processes.

sections.h3: Why the metrics matter in real life

blocks.text: A bank’s online portal must keep response time low so a user sees the transaction status instantly. The scheduler therefore prefers a preemptive policy that gives each request a short time slice.
A data‑center batch job that processes nightly reports cares more about throughput and CPU utilization. Here a non‑preemptive, high‑throughput policy may be chosen.

items: Mobile apps using UPI need fast response time to show payment confirmation.
Railway ticket booking (IRCTC) experiences many short requests; preemptive round robin keeps the queue moving.
A power‑cut in Chennai can be mitigated if critical control processes have high CPU utilization and low waiting time.

examples.question:
Two processes arrive at time 0. P1 has CPU burst = 6 ms, P2 has CPU burst = 4 ms.
(a) Compute waiting, turnaround and response times using FCFS (non‑preemptive).
(b) Compute the same metrics using Shortest‑Remaining‑Time‑First (preemptive).
steps: FCFS order: P1 runs first, then P2.
P1: waiting = 0 ms (starts immediately). Turnaround = 6 ms (0 + 6). Response = 0 ms.
P2: waiting = 6 ms (P1 runs 0‑6). Turnaround = 6 + 4 = 10 ms. Response = 6 ms.
SRTF order: at time 0 both are ready; P2 has shorter remaining time, so it runs first.
P2 runs 0‑4 ms, finishes. P1 then runs 4‑10 ms.
P1: waiting = 4 ms (starts at 4). Turnaround = 4 + 6 = 10 ms. Response = 4 ms.
P2: waiting = 0 ms. Turnaround = 4 ms. Response = 0 ms.
examples.answer: FCFS average waiting time = 3 ms; SRTF average waiting time = 2 ms.

traps: Adding turnaround time to waiting time instead of computing them separately; turnaround already includes waiting.
Using response time of the second process in FCFS as the system’s response time; response time is measured per process.
Confusing preemptive SRTF with non‑preemptive SJF; the former can switch when a shorter job arrives, the latter cannot.

quiz.a: CPU utilization = (time CPU is busy ÷ total elapsed time) × 100 %.

quiz.q: Why does a preemptive scheduler usually give lower average waiting time than a non‑preemptive one?
quiz.a: Because it can interrupt a long‑running process and run a shorter or higher‑priority process, reducing the time short jobs wait in the ready queue.

quiz.q: A system runs three processes with bursts 5 ms, 3 ms, 8 ms arriving at time 0. Using FCFS, compute the average turnaround time.
quiz.a: Order = 5,3,8. Completion times = 5,8,16 ms. Turnaround = 5,8,16 ms. Average = (5+8+16)/3 = 9.67 ms.

quiz.q: If a preemptive round‑robin scheduler uses a time‑slice of 2 ms, what is the worst‑case response time for a process that arrives just after the slice starts?
quiz.a: The process must wait for the current slice (2 ms) plus all other ready processes each getting a slice before its next turn. In the worst case with N‑1 other processes, response time = 2 ms × N.

quiz.q: What is the unit of throughput?
quiz.a: Jobs per hour (or per second, depending on the context).

quiz.q: Given bursts 4 ms and 7 ms arriving at time 0, compute average waiting time for SRTF.
quiz.a: Shorter burst (4 ms) runs first, waiting times = 0 ms and 4 ms. Average = (0+4)/2 = 2 ms.

beyond: Not for the exam. In cloud data‑centers, scheduling criteria are combined with energy‑aware metrics to reduce power consumption. Real‑time operating systems add deadline‑miss rate as a critical metric. Research explores machine‑learning‑based schedulers that predict burst lengths to improve all criteria. Look for papers on “adaptive CPU scheduling” and “energy‑performance trade‑offs” to see the latest developments.
